6 questions. Click an answer to check it: you will see right away whether it is correct, with a short explanation. Nothing is saved.

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**1.** What does the $R^2$ score measure?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The average error of the model, in the unit of the target
- The share of the variance of the target explained by the model
- The number of features used
- The correlation between two features
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
$R^2 = 1 - SSR/SST$: 1 means perfect predictions, 0 means no better than always predicting the mean. It can even be negative on a test set, when the model is worse than the mean.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**2.** A model has $R^2 = 0.97$ on the training set and $0.62$ on the test set. What is happening?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The model underfits
- The model overfits
- The test set is too large
- Everything is fine
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
A large gap between the training and test scores is the sign of overfitting: the model has learned details of the training data that don't generalize.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**3.** In the California housing exercise, two features (the nearest big city and the distance to it) improve the model as much as 40 polynomial features. What does it show?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Polynomial features are useless
- Features that bring knowledge about the problem are worth more than many mechanical ones
- Distances always improve models
- Linear regression can't use categorical features
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
Prices depend on **where** a district is, close to a big city or not. Encoding this knowledge directly is more effective than hoping the model finds it in powers of the latitude.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**4.** The features of a linear regression have been standardized. How can we compare their importance?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- With the raw values of the coefficients
- With the absolute values of the coefficients
- With the p-values only
- We can't compare them
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
On standardized features, a coefficient is the effect of a change of one standard deviation: their **absolute values** can be compared. A large negative coefficient is as important as a large positive one.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**5.** What does forward selection do?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- It removes the feature with the highest p-value at each step
- It starts with no feature and adds, at each step, the one that improves the model the most
- It tries every possible subset of features
- It creates new features
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
Forward selection adds features one by one (`SequentialFeatureSelector` in scikit-learn). Backward elimination does the opposite: it starts with all the features and removes them one by one.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**6.** Why can't we plot a linear regression with three features and the target?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Because the model is not linear anymore
- Because we would need four dimensions
- Because plotly can't plot regressions
- We can, with a scatter matrix
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
Three features plus the target make four dimensions. That's why metrics like $R^2$ are essential: most of the time we can't see the model.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-score}
